newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African trade-weighted rand leaps six pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: S.African trade-weighted rand leaps six pct in '97.

text.p: South Africa's trade-weighted rand has strengthened by almost six percent since the beginning of the year, providing a period of respite for importers ravaged by the currency's depreciation last year.

An indication of how much the South African rand has improved against the currencies of its major trading partners is provided by the Reserve Bank, which calculates a trade-weighed rand index incorporating the dollar, sterling, the Deutschmark and yen.
That index was indicated at 58.00 points on Monday -- a 5.95 percent improvement from the beginning of the year.
On an individual basis, the rand has stormed to its strongest levels against the yen and Deutschmark since April last year and is at a 3-1/2-month high against sterling and the U.S. dollar.
Foreign exchange traders have put the rand's improvement down to a surge in exporter dollar sales as well as a renewed inflow of offshore funds into the domestic gilts market
ING Barings economist Hania Farhan believes foreign perceptions of the country had been bolstered by a host of factors.

"Basically they believe that the fiscal deficit will come in on target, privatisation will be announced and while growth is low, they think that interest rates should fall and so set in place the scene for stronger growth in 1998," Farhan said.

Government has set itself a fiscal deficit target of 5.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 and there are indications that an announcement on the privatisation of certain state assets could be made in the budget on March 12.
Analysts believe that in the short-term, the rand's improvement could provide a fillip to imports.

In 1996, the trade-weighted rand depreciated by 23 percent, squeezing importers and helping the country post a 10.577 billion rand trade surplus for the year -- more than double 1995's total of 4.884 billion rand.

Charles Jonker at Absa Bank Treasury said that while it was premature to predict what impact the trade-weighted rand's improvement would have on the trade balance, coupled with the continuing reduction of tariffs, it could boost imports in the short-term.

"If (the rand) continues at these levels, then imports will move up. But I think that it is a bit premature to start arguing that it will have a detrimental effect on the trade balance in the sense that imports will start skyrocketing to the detriment of exports," Jonker said.
One economist noted that while the rand's improvement would make it cheaper to import, a sluggish economy would stymie any large-scale increase in imports.
South African gross domestic product growth is expected to slow to between 1.9 percent and 2.2 percent this year from around three percent in 1996 as consumer spending tails off.
The economist said that sluggish demand would thus reduce the country's propensity to import and offset the effects of cheaper import prices.

In early Monday afternoon trade, the rand was trading trading at 26.9131/9531 against the yen -- a level last seen on April 1, 1996 year -- and at 0.3634/3737 marks, its strongest since April 12 last year.
It was also quoted at 7.2603/2696 against sterling and at 4.5275/5305 against the dollar -- the strongest levels since mid-October.
